title: Commander in Chief for Life
author: John Kendall Hawkins
content:
![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/P20260103MR-0844_President_Donald_Trump_CIA_Director_John_Ratcliffe_Secretary_of_State_Marco_Rubio_and_Deputy_Chief_of_Staff_Stephen_Miller_monitor_U.S._military_operations_in_Venezuela-680x453.jpg)

Photograph Source: The White House - Public Domain

**I.**

Seymour Hersh reported yesterday that the White House has an operational plan
for November, and that the plan does not depend on persuading anyone.

The man running it, according to Hersh, is Stephen Miller, whose assignment is
to keep Democrats from taking Senate seats in a short list of contested
states: Alaska, Georgia, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire, North Carolina,
Ohio, Texas. The method has nothing to do with rooting out fraud. Hersh’s
sources describe a plan to station uniformed troops at polling places in the
closest races, with Marine Corps units directed toward precincts holding large
numbers of Black and Hispanic voters. Texas and Georgia are named. The theory
is that a certain number of citizens will see soldiers at the door of the
church basement and turn around. A source with firsthand political knowledge
told Hersh that discouraging even a handful at the right precincts could hold
a seat or take one.

That is the entire scheme. It needs no hacked tabulator, no slate of fake
electors, no Eastman memo. It needs a uniform standing in a doorway on a
Tuesday morning.

It also has a fallback, and the fallback is the part worth losing sleep over.
Soldiers at precincts can be enjoined, filmed, and converted into a turnout
drive for the other side. A war cannot. Since April this country has been
fighting one in Iran that the president started by himself, and a commander in
chief in the middle of a war he started is a very difficult man to remove.

Why now is no mystery. A national Emerson survey this week put the Democrats
eleven points up on the generic congressional ballot. Fox’s own poll gave them
seven, with Brit Hume conceding on air that his network’s numbers held nothing
good for Republicans. Trump’s approval sits at thirty-nine percent, the lowest
of either term. Kalshi has the House going Democratic at eighty-three percent.
If both chambers turn over, the new Congress will move on impeachment, and the
president knows it.

**II.** **The Option They Discarded**

The most instructive detail in Hersh’s account is the thing they decided
against.

In April, Senator Elissa Slotkin asked Pete Hegseth at an Armed Services
hearing whether he would deploy troops to seize ballots and voting machines on
election day if the president ordered it. Hegseth refused to answer,
dismissing the question as a gotcha hypothetical. Hersh now reports that the
White House election operatives concluded ballot seizure was not politically
viable and settled on intimidation instead.

They set it aside because they have never needed it.

Greg Palast has spent two decades documenting the quieter instrument, and his
findings have the tedious quality of real evidence. Interstate Crosscheck,
which flagged voters for removal on the strength of a shared name. Felon rolls
in Florida. Phantom moving in Georgia. Form irregularities in Ohio.
Provisional ballots issued and then discarded on technicalities the voter
never learns about. The MIT study Palast cites, Losing Votes by Mail, put
mail-in loss at twenty-two percent. I went through all of this in these pages
in November 2020, while the country watched CNN repeat itself and
congratulated itself on a count that had finally gone the other way. The
machinery that ate close to six million votes in 2016 was never dismantled. It
was, for one cycle, simply out-voted.

So the progression is legible. Purge the rolls and nobody sees it. Spoil the
mail-in ballots and nobody sees it. When the margin grows too wide for
paperwork to close, you send the Marines. The escalation from the clerk’s
office to the rifle company is an admission that the quiet method has run out
of room.

**III. The Vulnerability Nobody Wanted to Hear About**

Hersh writes that Trump’s speech last week about weaknesses in American
election infrastructure was largely false. He is right about the speech. It is
worth saying plainly that the underlying weakness is real, which is exactly
what makes it useful to this president.

At DefCon, invited hackers took apart voting machines then in use across
twenty-six states and demonstrated that compromising a single model could
swing an Electoral College outcome. Five days before the 2020 election,
machine problems in Pennsylvania and Georgia remained unaddressed. Those of us
who wrote about it were waved off as cranks, largely because the party best
positioned to fix it preferred the subject closed. Six years of official
indifference have now been handed to a man who intends to use them as a
pretext.

At the Nader and Fein impeachment symposium in the Senate Visitors Center on
July 22, Bruce Fein described the scenario without hedging. Sometime before
November, Trump declares a national emergency over compromised voting
machines, cites the Chinese vulnerabilities he has been advertising for a
week, and sends the military in to seize the machines and stop the count for
some unspecified duration. Fein observed that nobody in the room laughed.

**IV**. **Dress Rehearsals**

None of this arrives without practice. National Guard troops went into Los
Angeles, Portland, and Chicago over the objections of the governors of those
states. A federal judge in Portland barred them from the streets, and in
November 2025 permanently blocked the deployment after a three-day trial. The
Supreme Court declined to let the administration put Guard troops into the
Chicago area. Trump pulled them out of all three cities at the end of 2025 and
announced that he was doing so, while leaving the door open to sending federal
forces back in a stronger form.

The law here is not ambiguous. It is a crime to station troops or armed men at
any place where an election is held, unless the force is needed to repel armed
enemies of the United States. Military personnel are barred from interfering
with an election officer’s duties. The Posse Comitatus Act generally forbids
using the armed forces for domestic law enforcement. The Insurrection Act is
the exception that swallows the rule, and this administration has spent
eighteen months manufacturing the emergencies that would trigger it.

**V.****What the Pentagon Did in 1974**

The last president to face removal had a Pentagon that worried about exactly
this.

In the spring of 1974 a Washington bureaucrat named Joseph Laitin telephoned
Defense Secretary James Schlesinger and raised the possibility that Nixon
might mobilize Marines to save his presidency. If I were in your job, Laitin
told him, I would want to know where the combat troops nearest downtown
Washington are and whose orders they take. Schlesinger hung up on him. That
July he went to General George Brown, the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs, and
told him that any order arriving from the White House was to come to him
directly and immediately, and that no extraordinary measures were to be taken.
Brown later said the chain would have caught anything: troop orders pass
through a Pentagon command center, he would have known within two minutes, and
he would have been in the secretary’s office thirty seconds after that. Hersh
reported the Laitin call. The New York Times put the Pentagon’s precautions on
page one three weeks after Nixon resigned. Schlesinger also recalled Admiral
Zumwalt telling him that Nixon had asked the Joint Chiefs, the previous
Christmas, whether there was military support for keeping him in power.

Stanley Kutler argued for the rest of his life that the whole business was a
fable, that nothing beyond Schlesinger’s own account supports it, and that no
evidence ever surfaced of Nixon or his staff planning any such thing. Take
Kutler’s side of it. The relevant fact survives either way. In 1974 the
question of whether the armed forces might be used to keep a president in
office was speculative enough that serious historians could spend fifty years
calling it a rumor. And the institutional answer, real or imagined, came from
inside the building: a Secretary of Defense and a Chairman of the Joint Chiefs
who decided on their own initiative that their oath ran to the document rather
than to the man.

That brake has been removed on purpose. The current Secretary of Defense stood
in front of eight hundred generals and admirals at Quantico last September to
talk about purging the culture of the Pentagon, has spent the months since
clearing minorities and women out of the senior ranks, and when Slotkin asked
him in April whether he would send troops to seize ballots, declined to say.

Some of the uniformed resistance survives. On July 21, the day before the
Nader symposium, retired Lieutenant General H.R. McMaster told the House
Intelligence Committee that discussing the military’s role in the 2026
election is irresponsible, that the founders were most concerned about the
military becoming involved in politics, and that this kind of talk is
dangerous and damaging. Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi, who questioned
him, said the president’s willingness to discuss deploying troops to polling
places undermines one of the oldest traditions of American democracy. In June,
Slotkin introduced the Protect Our Polls Act, which would require a Joint
Resolution of Approval before a president could send troops or federal law
enforcement to election sites. With the midterms months away, legislative
solutions arrive too late.

**VI. The Alibi**

Troops at polling places is the crude instrument. Visible, illegal on its
face, litigable, and by Hersh’s own account as likely to put voters in the
street as to turn them away. The second mechanism is quieter and better
precedented, and the president already holds it.

The precedents are structural rather than moral. In Ukraine, martial law
extends every mandate and elections do not occur. Whatever one concludes about
Zelensky personally, the mechanism is indifferent to his character: a state at
war lawfully postpones its own accountability, on paper, with no coup
required. In Israel, Netanyahu has demonstrated the other half of the
equation. A prime minister under indictment who remains a war leader remains,
in practice, beyond the reach of the process against him, and Haaretz has said
in print what a good many Israelis suspect about whose interests are served by
the duration of the fighting.

Trump now has both halves. Since April the United States has been at war with
Iran, a war the president began on his own authority, without a declaration,
and which he escalated with a public promise to ninety million Iranians that
their civilization would end that night. Hegseth has been back to Congress for
another thirty-seven and a half billion dollars to continue it. Celinda Lake
told the symposium that the American public has concluded the war will run at
least another year. Nader, opening the day, raised the prospect of tactical
nuclear weapons. Fein said flatly that the president is without scruples where
nuclear war is concerned.

A commander in chief in the middle of a war he started, facing a Congress that
has surrendered the purse and a Supreme Court that has already granted him
immunity for official acts, does not need to cancel an election. He needs only
to be indispensable while it happens.

**VII. Impeachment Hushing**

The remedy has been sitting in Article II, Section 4 the entire time. Fein
likes to ask people who tell him impeachment is off the table whether they
have airbrushed it out of the Constitution.

Celinda Lake, who has been polling for Democrats since before most of the
current House leadership held office, brought the numbers to the Senate
Visitors Center on July 22, and they are not ambiguous. Impeachment runs
between 53 and 56 percent. Independents and swing voters favor it by more than
twenty points. Support tracks presidential job approval almost exactly, which
makes it stable, and Trump has done nothing that would raise his. Among those
who oppose impeachment, roughly a third concede the allegations may well be
true. Lake’s assessment of Beltway conventional wisdom on the question was
that it runs wrong close to a hundred percent of the time.

So why will House Democrats not put their names on H. Res. 1155? John Larson’s
thirteen articles, drafted with Fein’s assistance, have been available since
April.

Steve Cohen, serving his last term after the Tennessee legislature carved his
majority-Black district into three pieces at Trump’s request, described
sending his own impeachment resolution around for cosponsors. Repeatedly.
Forcefully. He collected two or three. Fein asked whether the money explained
it, and Cohen’s answer came to yes. Leadership controls the campaign
committee. Leadership controls your committee seats, whether your bill reaches
the floor, whether your amendment is heard. Fein called the refusal political
cowardice, which is the charitable reading. Hakeem Jeffries, asked by a
reporter about impeachment, said he did not want to get ahead of the
narrative. Ninety percent of Democratic voters are already there, along with
two-thirds of independents. He is behind his own narrative and calling it
strategy.

Kira Havens, an Air Force veteran who started Citizens Impeachment in April
2025, described going member to member asking whether they would use Rule
Nine, the provision that lets any member force a privileged resolution to the
floor within two legislative days. Al Green has done it twice. The answer she
kept getting was not until after the midterms. So she went out and recruited
people who would. Nineteen of them are on general election ballots in
November, in front of something like thirteen million voters. That is the
current price of getting the constitutional remedy onto a ballot at all: build
a slate from scratch, because the incumbents will not move.

There is a further wrinkle worth naming. The Constitution already contains the
disqualification power, in Article I, Section 3, which permits the Senate to
bar a convicted officeholder from any future office of honor, trust, or
profit. It has never bitten this president because it requires conviction, and
the Senate has twice declined to convict. The instrument is in the drawer.
Nobody will open the drawer.

Hersh opens the same door from the other side. At the end of his piece he
reports that longtime wealthy Democratic donors in New York and elsewhere are
alarmed. What alarms them is the party’s drift leftward, the prospect of
higher taxes should Democrats take Congress, and renewed calls among younger
members for guaranteed universal healthcare, which he says these donors regard
with horror. Marines outside precincts in Houston and Savannah do not appear
on the list.

**VIII.**

Set the two halves of the ledger side by side.

The White House has an operation with a manager, a target map, a discarded
first option, and a service branch assigned to specific neighborhoods in
specific states. It also has a war, begun in April without a declaration,
which the public now expects to run at least another year, and which nobody in
Congress has shown any inclination to defund.

The opposition has a constitutional remedy, majority public support for using
it, independents twenty points in favor, and a donor class that finds
universal healthcare more alarming than any of the above.

Trump does not have to cancel an election. That was always the least likely
version, and the tell is that his own people looked at ballot seizure and
decided against it as bad politics. What he needs is a Congress content to
remain the caboose, which is Fein’s word for it, and a war that makes him
indispensable while the returns come in. The first has been handed to him by
people who read the same polls Lake presented and concluded that silence is
the safe play. The second he started himself.

In 1974 a Secretary of Defense picked up a telephone to make certain the Army
would not be used to keep a cornered president in office. In 2026 the
Secretary of Defense will not answer the question when a senator asks it out
loud.

Everything after that is arithmetic, and it is being done right now, precinct
by precinct, in an office down the hall from the Oval.
